claim: The proposed memory system would promote information based on repeated use across sessions, aiming to keep a smaller set of context that remains useful when applied.
The speakers distinguish information or instructions that are repeatedly useful from a one-off action that an agent happened to remember and then applies too broadly.
A review queue for proposed memories should use an inbox people already check, such as Slack, rather than create another place they must visit.
A shared team context can learn recurring practices faster than individual context, while avoiding competing versions of the same rule.
A proposed memory should carry its source statements and task context so a human can judge why the system suggested it.
Human feedback should be able to revise or merge a proposed rule, not only allow it or block it, and that feedback can retrigger the memory pipeline.
A small background process can have multiple triggers, such as a scheduled batch run, a Slack message, or feedback on an existing memory.
The described supervisor checks a written design document after a tool call and injects a workflow nudge only when a small model finds that the relevant design decisions are resolved.
The speakers recommend spending freely on a useful supporting agent first, then treating cost as an optimization problem once it becomes a real bottleneck.
note: This is a stated engineering preference, not a measured cost result.
